notes_list.title: Context Before Dictionary Meaning
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Never depend only on the first dictionary meaning of a word.
• Read the complete sentence and identify the contextual meaning.
• Check whether the word is being used positively, negatively, literally or figuratively.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 In competitive exams, a familiar word may be used in an unfamiliar sense. Context should be the first source of interpretation.

notes_list.title: Do Not Memorise Words in Isolation
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Learn a word with its meaning, synonym, antonym, common collocation and one example sentence.
• Group related words instead of memorising random lists.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: abundant → plentiful → scarce as antonym → abundant resources. Learning the word network improves recall.

notes_list.title: Active vs Passive Vocabulary
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Passive vocabulary: words recognised while reading.
• Active vocabulary: words that can be correctly used in speech or writing.
• Competitive exams mainly test recognition, meaning and usage, but active practice strengthens recall.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Write short original sentences using difficult words to convert recognition into usable knowledge.

notes_list.title: Meaning First, Option Second
notes_list.basic_overview:
• First determine the meaning of the given word.
• Then compare the options with that meaning.
• Do not simply choose an option that looks familiar.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 If the exact meaning is uncertain, identify whether the word expresses a positive, negative, neutral, intense or mild idea.

notes_list.title: Degree of Meaning
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Two words can be related but differ in intensity.
• Select the option closest in meaning and grammatical usage.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: angry and furious are related, but furious indicates stronger intensity.

notes_list.title: Part of Speech Check
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Check whether the question word is a noun, verb, adjective or adverb.
• Prefer an option that matches both meaning and grammatical category.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: rapid is an adjective, while rapidly is an adverb. A synonym must fit the required grammatical role.

notes_list.title: Root Word Method
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Break unfamiliar words into familiar roots, prefixes and suffixes.
• Use the likely meaning to eliminate unrelated options.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: bene- relates to good/well; mal- relates to bad; anti- indicates against; pre- indicates before.

notes_list.title: Positive-Negative Elimination
notes_list.basic_overview:
• If the exact meaning is unknown, first determine the emotional or semantic direction of the word.
• Eliminate options with the opposite direction.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 This method does not guarantee the answer, but it can reduce the options when exact recall fails.

notes_list.title: Understand the Exact Meaning
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Identify the exact sense of the given word before searching for its opposite.
• A word can have different antonyms depending on context.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: 'light' may oppose heavy, dark or serious depending on its context.

notes_list.title: True Opposite vs Related Word
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A related word is not necessarily an antonym.
• Look for a word that reverses or directly contrasts the relevant meaning.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: generous and kind are related ideas, but neither is necessarily the direct antonym of the other.

notes_list.title: Prefix-Based Antonyms
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Some opposites are formed using prefixes such as un-, in-, im-, ir-, il-, dis- and non-.
• However, not every word accepts every negative prefix.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: possible → impossible, regular → irregular, legal → illegal, honest → dishonest.

notes_list.title: Identify the Core Definition
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Read the complete definition carefully.
• Identify the key concept, person, action, place or condition being described.
• Then match it with the exact vocabulary term.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: One who loves mankind → philanthropist. One who hates mankind → misanthrope.

notes_list.title: Person-Based One Word Substitutions
notes_list.basic_overview:
• One who speaks many languages → polyglot.
• One who knows everything → omniscient.
• One who loves books → bibliophile.
• One who hates mankind → misanthrope.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📚 Learn one-word substitutions in semantic groups rather than alphabetically.

notes_list.title: Place, Practice & Concept Based Words
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Place-related, practice-related and concept-related substitutions should be learned separately.
• Pay attention to subtle differences between similar definitions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Grouping improves recall: government, professions, places, beliefs, habits, time periods and conditions.

notes_list.title: Do Not Interpret Literally
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Idioms often have meanings different from the literal meanings of their individual words.
• Learn the complete expression as a unit.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: 'Break the ice' means to initiate conversation or reduce social tension, not literally break ice.

notes_list.title: Use the Sentence Context
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Read the sentence containing the idiom.
• Determine what meaning fits the situation, action and tone.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Context can distinguish between options that look similar in meaning.

notes_list.title: Idioms as Situations
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Memorise an idiom together with the situation in which it is used.
• This is more effective than memorising only its Hindi translation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: 'Once in a blue moon' → something happening very rarely.

notes_list.title: Verb + Particle Changes Meaning
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A phrasal verb consists of a verb plus a particle or preposition.
• The combination may have a meaning different from the original verb.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: give up = quit; look after = take care of; carry on = continue.

notes_list.title: Separable & Inseparable Phrasal Verbs
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Some phrasal verbs allow the object to come between the verb and particle.
• Others do not.
• Pronoun objects often follow specific placement rules.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: turn off the light / turn the light off / turn it off. Not: turn off it.

notes_list.title: Look for Letter Patterns
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Pay attention to common spelling patterns, silent letters, double consonants and vowel combinations.
• Compare every option letter by letter when necessary.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Commonly tested examples include accommodation, separate, necessary, privilege, pronunciation and questionnaire.

notes_list.title: Double Letter Traps
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Many spelling questions test whether a consonant or vowel is doubled correctly.
• Break the word into syllables and compare familiar word families.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: accommodation has double c and double m.

notes_list.title: British & Exam-Oriented Spellings
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Competitive exams in India may use British/Indian English conventions.
• Be familiar with common forms such as colour, centre, labour and programme.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Always follow the spelling convention used by the particular examination and question source.

notes_list.title: Accept & Except
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Accept: receive or agree to.
• Except: excluding.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: I accept your proposal. Everyone came except Ravi.

notes_list.title: Affect & Effect
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Affect: commonly used as a verb meaning influence.
• Effect: commonly used as a noun meaning result.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: The decision affected the result. The effect was significant.

notes_list.title: Principal & Principle
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Principal: chief/head or a sum of money.
• Principle: fundamental rule or belief.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Memory aid: principal can be a person or principal amount; principle is a rule or belief.

notes_list.title: Compliment & Complement
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Compliment: praise.
• Complement: something that completes or goes well with something else.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: She complimented my work. The sauce complements the dish.

notes_list.title: Stationary & Stationery
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Stationary: not moving.
• Stationery: writing materials.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Memory aid: stationery → e for envelopes.

notes_list.title: Common Latin & Greek Roots
notes_list.basic_overview:
• bio → life
• geo → earth
• chron → time
• graph → write/record
• phon → sound
• scope → look/examine
• dict → say/speak
• aud → hear
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: biography, geography, chronology, autograph, telephone, microscope, predict, audible.

notes_list.title: Use Roots to Guess Meaning
notes_list.basic_overview:
• When a word is unfamiliar, identify any familiar root.
• Combine the root meaning with the context to estimate the word's meaning.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Root analysis is an elimination tool, not a guarantee. English words can develop meanings that differ from their original roots.

notes_list.title: Common Prefixes
notes_list.basic_overview:
• anti- → against
• pre- → before
• post- → after
• inter- → between
• trans- → across/change
• sub- → under
• super- → above/beyond
• mis- → wrongly
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: antisocial, preview, postgraduate, international, transport, submarine, supernatural, misunderstand.

notes_list.title: Common Suffixes
notes_list.basic_overview:
• -less → without
• -ful → full of
• -able → capable of
• -tion → action/process
• -ness → state/quality
• -ment → result/process
• -ist → person associated with an activity or belief
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: hopeless, useful, readable, education, kindness, development, scientist.

notes_list.title: Definition Clue
notes_list.basic_overview: • Sometimes the sentence directly explains an unfamiliar word through a definition or restatement.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Look for signals such as 'that is', 'meaning', 'in other words' and explanatory phrases.

notes_list.title: Example Clue
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Examples following an unfamiliar word can reveal its meaning.
• Look for phrases such as for example, such as and for instance.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example-based clues are especially useful in reading comprehension and cloze tests.

notes_list.title: Contrast Clue
notes_list.basic_overview: • Contrast markers can reveal the approximate opposite or contrasting meaning of an unfamiliar word.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Watch for however, but, although, unlike, whereas, in contrast and nevertheless.

notes_list.title: Cause & Effect Clue
notes_list.basic_overview: • The cause or consequence of an unfamiliar word can help identify its meaning.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Look for because, therefore, hence, as a result, due to and consequently.

notes_list.title: Read the Whole Passage First
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Do not solve every blank independently.
• Read enough surrounding text to understand the overall theme and logical direction.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 A later sentence may provide a clue for an earlier blank.

notes_list.title: Grammar + Vocabulary Together
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Determine whether the blank requires a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition or conjunction.
• Then select the option that fits both grammar and meaning.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 A word can be semantically suitable but grammatically impossible.

notes_list.title: Collocation Check
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Some words naturally occur together.
• Check whether the option forms a standard English expression with neighbouring words.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: make a decision, heavy rain, strong argument, deeply concerned.

notes_list.title: Make vs Do
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Common combinations with make: make a decision, make a mistake, make an effort, make progress.
• Common combinations with do: do work, do homework, do business, do research.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Learn collocations as complete chunks rather than isolated verb meanings.

notes_list.title: Strong & Heavy Collocations
notes_list.basic_overview: • Common expressions: strong argument, strong evidence, strong possibility, heavy rain, heavy traffic, heavy burden.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Collocation knowledge helps in fillers, sentence improvement, cloze tests and vocabulary questions.

notes_list.title: SSC Vocabulary Approach
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Prioritise synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitutions, idioms, spelling and contextual vocabulary.
• Build a revision list from repeated mistakes.
• Use elimination when exact recall is unavailable.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 For vocabulary questions, speed matters because many questions can be solved quickly when the word is familiar.

notes_list.title: DSSSB Vocabulary Approach
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Focus on practical vocabulary, synonyms, antonyms, idioms, spelling and usage.
• Read the full sentence before selecting a contextual meaning.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Keep separate revision groups for direct vocabulary and vocabulary appearing inside passages.

notes_list.title: UPSC Context-Based Vocabulary
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Context and comprehension are more important than memorising very large isolated word lists.
• Identify how a word functions in the author's argument.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 When vocabulary appears inside comprehension, prioritise the meaning supported by the passage rather than a memorised definition.

notes_list.title: Banking Vocabulary Approach
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Give special attention to contextual vocabulary, cloze tests, fillers, synonyms, antonyms and word usage.
• Learn common collocations and formal English expressions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Editorial-style English frequently rewards understanding of context, tone and collocation.

notes_list.title: Fast Vocabulary Method
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Build high-frequency vocabulary.
• Practise direct meaning, synonym, antonym, spelling and idiom questions.
• Use elimination for unfamiliar words.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Maintain a short revision notebook containing only repeatedly missed or frequently tested words.

notes_list.title: Opposite Meaning Elimination
notes_list.basic_overview:
• If the question asks for a synonym and an option is clearly opposite in meaning, eliminate it.
• The same principle applies in reverse for antonyms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 First eliminate clearly incompatible options, then compare the remaining choices.

notes_list.title: Wrong Part of Speech
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Eliminate an option if its grammatical category does not match the required word.
• Check noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: beauty and beautiful are related but cannot always replace each other because their grammatical roles differ.

notes_list.title: Wrong Intensity
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A word may be related in meaning but too weak or too strong for the question.
• Compare intensity and semantic precision.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: irritated, angry and furious express increasing intensity in many contexts.

notes_list.title: Context Mismatch
notes_list.basic_overview:
• An option may be a valid dictionary meaning but unsuitable in the given sentence.
• Reject options that do not fit the surrounding context.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Context mismatch is especially important in passage, cloze and sentence-based vocabulary questions.

notes_list.title: Word Family Method
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Learn related forms together.
• Example: decide → decision → decisive → decisively.
• This builds multiple usable forms from one root.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Word families are useful for error detection, fillers, cloze tests and sentence improvement.

notes_list.title: Synonym-Antonym Pairing
notes_list.basic_overview: • Learn a difficult word together with at least one synonym and one antonym whenever possible.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: abundant → plentiful → scarce as antonym.

notes_list.title: Sentence Association
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Create a short meaningful sentence using the new word.
• Personal or familiar situations can make recall easier.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 A word remembered through meaning + usage is generally easier to recognise later than a word memorised only through translation.

notes_list.title: Spaced Revision
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Revise difficult vocabulary at increasing intervals rather than repeatedly reading the same list in one sitting.
• Keep separate lists for new, uncertain and mastered words.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Suggested cycle: same day → next day → several days later → weekly review → periodic mixed revision.

notes_list.title: Daily Word Learning
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Learn a manageable number of new words.
• Revise previously learned words.
• Solve synonym, antonym and contextual questions.
• Record mistakes.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Consistency is more useful than memorising a very large list once and never revising it.

notes_list.title: Error Notebook
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Record words answered incorrectly or guessed incorrectly.
• Write meaning, synonym, antonym, example sentence and the reason for the mistake.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 The error notebook should contain personal weak areas rather than reproducing an entire dictionary.

notes_list.title: Mixed Revision
notes_list.basic_overview: • Mix synonyms, antonyms, idioms, one-word substitutions, spellings, phrasal verbs and contextual vocabulary during revision.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🧠 Mixed practice improves the ability to identify which vocabulary rule a question is testing.

notes_list.title: Before Selecting an Option
notes_list.basic_overview:
• What is the exact meaning of the word?
• What is its part of speech?
• What is the context?
• Is the option a true synonym/antonym?
• Is the intensity appropriate?
• Does the option fit grammatically?
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Meaning → Context → Part of Speech → Intensity → Option comparison.

notes_list.title: If the Word Is Unknown
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Look for a familiar root.
• Check prefix/suffix.
• Determine positive/negative/neutral sense.
• Use nearby context.
• Eliminate clearly incompatible options.
notes_list.extra_info_content: ⚠️ Guessing should be evidence-based rather than purely random.

notes_list.title: Golden Vocabulary Rule
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Do not learn vocabulary only by translation.
• Learn word + meaning + usage + synonym + antonym + context.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📚 The objective is recognition and correct usage in the kinds of contexts encountered in competitive examinations.
